question: What is the Open/Closed Principle?
title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP) — open for extension, closed for modification
direct_answer: **OCP** states that a class should be **open for extension but closed for modification**. You should be able to add new behavior by **adding new code** (a new class or implementation), not by **changing existing working code**. Changing existing code risks breaking what already works.

The shape area example is classic. You have one method with if-else for circle, rectangle, triangle. Adding a pentagon means touching that method again, re-testing it, and risking the three shapes that already worked.

sharp edge: these chains are called the type-switching antipattern. Interviewers love it as a code smell question. The fix is always the same: make each type its own class with an area method, so adding a new shape is just adding a new class.

question: What is the problem with long if-else chains in terms of OCP?
title: If-else chains as OCP violations
direct_answer: Long if-else or switch chains that check a type to decide behavior are **OCP violations**. Every time you add a new type, you must **modify** the existing if-else block. This is risky, error-prone, and violates the closed-for-modification rule. The fix is polymorphism — each type becomes its own class.

sections.content: Long if-else chains checking a type string are a classic OCP violation. Every time a new type is added, someone has to find this method, open it, add another branch, and hope they did not break anything. The better design is to let each type be its own class with the behavior defined in a method. Then adding a new type means adding a new file — nothing existing is touched or risked.

question: Which design patterns are commonly used to achieve OCP?
title: Design patterns that implement the Open/Closed Principle
direct_answer: The most common patterns for OCP are: **Strategy** (swap algorithms via interface), **Template Method** (define steps in base class, vary steps in subclasses), **Decorator** (add behavior by wrapping), and **Factory** (create objects without hardcoding types). Each allows extension without modifying existing code.

sections.title: OCP-enabling patterns
sections.content: Strategy: extract variable behavior into an interface; add new strategies as new classes. Template Method: define the skeleton in a base class; subclasses override only what varies. Decorator: wrap an object to add behavior without changing the original. Factory/Abstract Factory: create objects by type without if-else in the consuming code. All four share the same mechanism: depend on abstractions so you can extend by adding implementations.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: The Strategy pattern is the most direct OCP implementation — you define an interface for the behavior that varies and create a new class for each strategy. The Template Method pattern also applies OCP at the inheritance level, where the base class defines the structure and subclasses add variations. Decorator adds behavior by wrapping without modifying the original. All of these patterns follow the same idea: depend on abstractions so new behavior comes from new code, not changed code.

question: Does OCP mean you should never modify existing code?
title: OCP and code modification — what is actually closed?
direct_answer: No. **OCP does not mean never touch existing code**. It means stable, well-tested code should not need to change just to add new features. **Bug fixes, refactoring, and performance improvements** still require modifying code. The key is: adding a new feature should ideally be done by adding new code, not by editing already-working code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Nuanced understanding of OCP — it is a guideline, not a law
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Interpreting OCP as a blanket prohibition on touching code

sections.title: What closed really means
sections.content: Closed for modification means: once a class is tested and in production, you should not need to reopen it every time a new feature is added. It is not about bug fixes — those always require modifying code. It is about design: if your design is extensible, new features are additive. OCP is a goal to strive for in design, not a hard rule that forbids ever editing a file.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: OCP does not mean you can never modify code. Bugs get fixed, code gets refactored, performance improves — all of that requires changes. What OCP is really saying is: design your classes so that adding new features does not require changing already-working, already-tested code. If every new business requirement forces you to edit three existing classes, your design is not extensible. The goal is additive change — new feature, new file.
